tldr: We present a framework that automatically builds a high-fidelity simulation environment using 3D Gaussian Splatting from a smartphone room video and object photos, adapting a pretrained VLA policy to a specific environment without any robot teleoperation. A model fine-tuned entirely on simulation-generated data achieves a 63.9% pickup success rate on a real Stretch 3 robot.
hero_caption: The overall workflow of Splat2Act. With just a smartphone scan of the room and photos of the objects, a simulatable digital twin is constructed, completing everything from grasp demonstration generation to personalized VLA adaptation without any teleoperation.
overview:
Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models hold strong potential for manipulating objects across diverse environments. However, the reality is harsh: even a powerful foundation model like $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves a 0% pickup success rate when brought directly into an individual home or office without adaptation, due to differences in placement locations and object appearances. Collecting data via human teleoperation for every deployment site to solve this is prohibitively expensive.

Therefore, the authors developed "Splat2Act," an automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that reduces human effort to merely scanning a room for 20–30 minutes with a smartphone and taking photos of the target objects, while automating the rest of the training pipeline. By combining 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS: a technique that represents realistic 3D appearance using multiple Gaussian functions) with mesh extraction, it builds a digital twin of the entire room. Furthermore, it automatically discovers placeable surfaces (receptacles) from geometry and automatically generates successful trajectories using a privileged oracle inside the simulator.

In experiments, the pipeline extracted 852 receptacles from 101 indoor environments and automatically generated over 68,000 demonstrations. Through a two-stage fine-tuning process using these demonstrations, the policy recorded a 62.5% pickup success rate in simulation and 63.9% on a real Stretch 3 robot. This breakthrough demonstrates that adaptation to an individual environment is possible using only a high-quality digital twin and automatically generated in-simulation data, without collecting any additional demonstrations on the real robot.
contributions: Built an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that takes only smartphone capture of a room and objects as input, fully automating task definition and demonstration generation without requiring any human teleoperation.
Constructed a large-scale simulation dataset by automatically discovering 852 receptacles across 101 building-scale indoor environments and collecting over 68,000 successful pickup demonstrations.

Fine-tuned a pretrained VLA ($\pi_{0.5}$) by combining broad simulation adaptation with scene-specific personalization, achieving a 63.9% pickup success rate on a real robot (Stretch 3) and revealing its effectiveness and generalization characteristics.

sections.heading: Why does even a powerful VLA fail right out of the box?
sections.summary: Pretrained VLAs face the harsh reality of a 0% pickup success rate without site adaptation. Meanwhile, the conventional approach of collecting teleoperation demonstrations in every home is prohibitively expensive. This study proposes a pipeline that automatically generates building-scale digital twins and demonstrations using only smartphone captures, personalizing the VLA.
sections.details:
When deploying a mobile manipulator in a home or office, we expect it to follow natural instructions like "pick up the medicine bottle from the shelf" or "pick up the soup can from the side table." Modern VLA models claim such open-world capabilities, but they struggle completely when deployed directly on site. In the paper's experiments, testing the strong pretrained model $\pi_{0.5}$ directly in deployment environments yielded a pickup success rate of 0.0%.

Normally, bridging this gap requires fine-tuning on additional data collected via human teleoperation or interventions on site, but repeating this process whenever users, furniture, or objects change is unrealistic.

Conventional real-to-sim methods (approaches that reproduce real environments in simulation) have improved visual fidelity using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), but most were limited to single tabletop scales or required human annotations. This scale is insufficient for mobile manipulators that roam freely across entire rooms.

To solve this, this study proposes "Splat2Act." All the user has to do is scan the entire room for 20–30 minutes with a handheld smartphone and provide photos and dimensions of the target objects. No robot setup or expert teleoperation is needed. From this data, the system automatically builds a high-fidelity digital twin of the entire room in simulation, discovers reachable locations for the robot, and automatically generates large volumes of pickup demonstration data.

sections.heading: How does it differ from existing Real-to-Sim? From single tables to entire rooms and personalization
sections.summary: While research on VLA adaptation and automated data generation is thriving, conventional 3DGS-based real-to-sim has remained at the single tabletop scale. Splat2Act sets itself apart by geometrically analyzing building-scale environments to autonomously discover receptacles, focusing specifically on adapting to individual environments.
sections.details:
### II-A VLA Models and Adaptation Methods
The emergence of OpenVLA, $\pi_{0}$, and $\pi_{0.5}$ has laid the foundation for generalist manipulation policies. However, no matter how broadly they are pretrained, adapting to downstream new environments and robot embodiments is essential. This work addresses the setting of adapting a VLA to both user-specific objects and deployment scene appearances as well as reachable placements.

### II-B Automated Data Generation and Deployment-Specific Data
Because large-scale real-world data collection (such as Open X-Embodiment) has limitations, automated data generation using simulation, such as GenSim and RoboTwin, is attracting attention. However, for scene-specific personalization, data must be grounded in the actual environment where the robot operates.

### II-C Real-to-Sim-to-Real Manipulation
Real-to-sim works that scan real environments into simulators include RialTo, DREAM, PRISM, and SplatSim. However, these mostly targeted a single tabletop. In addition, recent works like LEGS and VLK handle room scales, but they required humans to annotate or specify target object locations and work surfaces in advance.

Splat2Act differs significantly from these in two ways. The first is "scale." It covers massive building-scale spaces with a median navigable area of 104.87 $\mathrm{m^2}$, and fully automatically discovers diverse receptacles such as shelves, not just tables, based on geometry. The second is that "its goal is personalization." Beyond automated task generation, it thoroughly investigates how scene-specific data and multi-scene data impact VLA adaptation.

sections.heading: From smartphone scan to real-robot deployment: Splat2Act's fully automated pipeline
sections.summary: 3DGS and meshes are extracted from smartphone video, reachable receptacles are autonomously discovered, and pickup tasks are assembled. A privileged oracle inside the simulator automatically generates pickup motions, which are used to fine-tune the pretrained VLA in two stages.
sections.details:
Splat2Act is designed for Hello Robot's mobile manipulator, the "Stretch 3." The overall pipeline consists of the following components:

### III-A Scene and Object Representation
From an RGB-D sequence captured by a user over 20–30 minutes using an iPhone app (Polycam), DN-Splatter is used to learn a 3DGS representation while maintaining geometric consistency. Furthermore, SuGaR is used to extract a surface-aligned mesh from the Gaussian representation. This establishes a hybrid environment balancing "ultra-realistic first-person visuals via 3DGS" and "collision detection and geometric analysis via meshes." For objects, 556 assets selected from Objaverse are used for broad adaptation, while 3D meshes generated from a single smartphone photo using SAM3D are used for personalization.

### III-B Receptacle Discovery and Task Construction
The floor plane is estimated from the extracted mesh, and upward-facing planar regions are detected based on the robot's physical dimensions. After clustering with HDBSCAN to identify stable receptacles, the robot's navigation mesh (NavMesh) is computed using the Habitat simulator. Candidate placement locations reachable within the robot's reach (within a 0.70 m radius) are sampled, automatically constructing feasible tasks.

### III-C Automated Demonstration Generation via Privileged Oracle
Parallel environments are launched on Isaac Sim to run a privileged oracle (scripted control) with ground-truth object poses and geometric knowledge. It moves the arm toward precomputed grasp candidate poses and includes a retry mechanism that rewinds the state and tries alternative candidates if a grasp fails. On a single A40 GPU across 64 parallel environments, it autonomously generates an average of 60 successful demonstrations per hour.

### III-D Two-Stage Policy Adaptation
A two-stage supervised fine-tuning (SFT) scheme is used to fine-tune the pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$. Stage 1 performs broad adaptation using public object assets (from either the deployment scene alone or all 101 scenes), and Stage 2 performs personalization tailored to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. The image encoder (SigLIP) is frozen, while the language model (PaliGemma) and Action Expert are fully fine-tuned across all layers.

### III-E Real-World Deployment
During real-world deployment, the robot's camera images and state are sent to a remote A40 GPU server, and inferred action chunks are received via gRPC for synchronous execution.

sections.heading: A dataset of 68,000 pickup demonstrations extracted from 101 campus spaces
sections.summary: From 101 building-scale environments across a university campus (totaling approximately 12,000 m²), 852 receptacles were identified and 68,021 successful pickup trajectories were generated. For evaluation, two scenes—an office and a conference room—and seven real objects were selected, with hard conditions including nearby distractor objects.
sections.details:
### IV-A Scale of Scenes and Demonstrations
The collected environments encompass 101 real indoor scenes on a university campus, including lounges, kitchens, and libraries. The total navigable area is 11,909.78 $\mathrm{m^2}$, with a median scene area of 104.87 $\mathrm{m^2}$ and a median of 7 receptacles per scene. Oracle generation yielded a total of 68,021 successful pickup trajectories (273.46 hours of total control time). While the potential task space reaches tens of millions, it is subsampled by roughly 1/100 for storage constraints.

Two scenes, "Office" and "Conference," were selected for personalization evaluation, alongside seven common real-world objects (medicine bottle, spam can, tomato soup can, cardboard box, Rubik's cube, spray can, and water bottle).

### IV-B Data for Broad Adaptation and Personalization
For Stage 1 (broad adaptation), two subsets of 1,024 demonstrations each were prepared:
- **Office1k**: Data covering 550 Objaverse objects exclusively within the Office environment.
- **Multi1k**: Data covering 556 objects across all 101 scenes and 852 receptacles.

In Stage 2 (personalization), three of the seven objects (medicine bottle, spam can, tomato soup can) serve as targets, while the remainder serve as distractor objects. 504 demonstrations were generated in Office and 500 in Conference, with 24 to 28 augmentations per pair.

### IV-C Evaluation Protocol
Each task has two conditions: "Easy," where only the target object is present, and "Hard," where distractors are scattered around it. Success is determined by whether the robot correctly lifts the target and the policy issues a termination command, calculating an exact success rate (SR) that accounts for failed attempts.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Remarkable adaptation in simulation and high-fidelity transfer to real robots
sections.summary: The model personalized after broad adaptation in the same environment achieved the highest performance, reaching a 62.5% success rate in the office scene. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Stretch 3 robot recorded a 63.9% success rate, demonstrating extremely close alignment between simulation and real-world performance.
sections.details:
### V-B Scaling Laws for Receptacles and Data Augmentation
Investigating variations in the number of receptacles and augmented tasks per object in Stage 2 revealed that requiring more receptacles and objects demands more trajectories. While success rates languished at 21.9–43.8% with around 8 tasks, augmenting to 24 or more tasks per object-receptacle pair significantly improved success rates to 75.0–87.5%.

### V-C Impact of Data Sources for Broad Adaptation
Simulation evaluation results are shown in Figure F3. Unadapted $\pi_{0.5}$ achieved a 0.0% success rate. In the office environment, the best-performing policy was trained in the order of "Office1k (same-environment broad adaptation) -> Office-specific personalization," reaching a 62.5% success rate. This is 17.5 percentage points higher than directly personalizing from the base model (45.0%). In the conference room, "Multi1k -> Conference personalization" achieved the highest score at 51.4%.
Additionally, under the Hard condition with surrounding distractors, directly personalized models suffered large drops in accuracy, whereas models that went through Stage 1 retained their language grounding ability and operated robustly.

### V-D Importance of Scene Personalization (Cross-Scene Evaluation)
When testing "policies personalized for a different room," success rates plummeted to 15.0–37.1% (Figure F5). Surprisingly, when evaluated in the office, the "policy personalized for the conference room (15.0%)" performed substantially worse than the "policy stopped at Office1k without any personalization (40.0%)." In other words, adapting only to objects while mismatched to the background environment actually hurts performance.

### V-E Sim-to-Real Transfer on Real Stretch 3
Twelve tasks in the office environment were evaluated on the real robot (3 trials each, 36 total). The policy personalized from Office1k achieved a 63.9% success rate on the real robot, closely tracking its 66.7% success rate in simulation (Figure F4). Although arm extension accuracy was slightly lower on the real robot than in simulation, the gripper's compliance and the friction of the rubber fingertips tolerated slight misalignments and aided successful grasps.

### V-F Generalization to Unseen Environments
When tested in an unseen laboratory (with a black desk and a yellow desk) not included in training, success rates dropped to the 20–30% range. While models adapted to a single scene were fragile to environmental changes, the Multi1k-based model trained on diverse 101 scenes exhibited more stable resilience across desk variations.

captions.F3: Simulation evaluation results on personalized tasks. Compared to the unadapted base model (0%), the policy personalized after broad adaptation in the same environment (dark orange) achieves the highest accuracy in Office at 62.5%.
captions.F4: Sim-to-real evaluation results using the real Stretch 3 robot. (a) shows that simulation and real success rates are at very close levels, and the scatter plot in (b) shows both performances closely tracking the parity line (dotted line).
captions.F5: Cross-evaluation results of policies personalized for different scenes. Personalizing for a room different from the target environment causes success rates to drop markedly, highlighting that adapting to the appearance of the environment itself is critical.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: Achieving personalized VLA adaptation without real-robot operations
sections.summary: Splat2Act successfully adapts VLAs to individual environments by automatically generating building-scale simulation spaces and demonstrations using only smartphone captures. By demonstrating that the sim-to-real gap can be crossed without collecting additional real-world demonstrations, this approach serves as a strong stepping stone toward widespread domestic robotics.
sections.details:
This study presented "Splat2Act," an automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that adapts VLA policies to individual environments and objects while eliminating all human effort beyond smartphone scanning.

The work demonstrated the ability to automatically extract receptacles from building-scale indoor spaces, synthesize tens of thousands of pickup demonstrations, and show that policies trained in simulation transfer directly to a real mobile manipulator (Stretch 3). In particular, the training design combining broad adaptation in the same environment with personalized fine-tuning proved key to unlocking high success rates (63.9%) on the real robot.

Looking ahead, the authors discuss extending the approach to longer-horizon mobile manipulation tasks (such as tidying up involving long-distance navigation across rooms) and incorporating reinforcement learning (RL) to further improve success rates through self-exploration.

takeaways: To run foundation VLA models on site, adaptation to both "environmental appearance" and "robot embodiment" is essential; a success rate of 0% without adaptation can be boosted to over 60% using only simulation data.

The framework has reached practical viability, going beyond single desks to building-scale 3DGS + mesh reconstruction, autonomously discovering receptacles, and generating pickup demonstrations fully automatically with a privileged oracle.

A two-stage training scheme that first performs "broad adaptation on diverse objects in the same room (Stage 1)" followed by "personalization to user-specific objects (Stage 2)" is the most effective.

Applying a policy personalized for a different environment degrades performance below that of an unadapted state, showing that adapting to the visual context of the placement environment, not just the objects, is critical.
limitations: Target tasks are currently limited to localized, short-horizon tasks of picking up a single object from a receptacle.
It is not entirely zero-effort, as smartphone scanning of a room takes 20–30 minutes, and objects require individual still photos and 3D meshing (SAM3D).

Because adaptation is specialized to a specific deployment site, generalization performance drops significantly to the 20–30% range when the robot is moved to unseen environments (OOD rooms or new desks).
